summary.title: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Aviation
summary.one_liner: A list of common but wrong assumptions programmers make about flights, airports, airlines, navigation data, and ADS-B transponder messages, useful when designing aviation data schemas.
takeaways: Flight numbers, airport codes, and airline codes are not one-to-one; an identifier can be ambiguous or change over time.
Airports can have multiple IATA codes or move, and runways and terminal or gate naming are not consistent.
ADS-B data can contain wrong positions, wrong flight IDs, wrong aircraft types, and false messages, so it should not be trusted blindly.
Flight plan and ANSP data can be edited, cancelled, or diverted, so status fields need careful interpretation.
Treat aviation identifiers and timing as messy real-world data when writing schemas and validation.
summary.summary: This FlightAware Engineering article lists false assumptions programmers commonly make about aviation data, modeled on Patrick McKenzie's essay about names. The items are grouped into sections on flights, airports, airlines, navigation, and transponders/ADS-B, each stating a belief followed by the reality, often with real examples like UAL1234 and B6459. The author notes that some of these have affected FlightAware's customers and internal systems, and that they illustrate what their Hyperfeed flight tracking engine must handle. It is a list of pitfalls rather than a tutorial, with no code or step-by-step instructions.
